solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: A leak requires record 50 euros spent

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record

indicators.note: money that is spent is gone and scattered, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written, then shuffled

explanation.surface: A political leak story: someone wants a payment of fifty euros on the record.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is an unauthorised revelation of information, which is a kind of disclosure.

clue.text: Half of a comedy act, Socialists' leader, Brown

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of Socialists
tan is a light brown colour

explanation.surface: A list of names: a comic double act, the head of the Socialists and Gordon Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: Stan Laurel was one half of the comedy double act Laurel and Hardy; Brown here is a colour, not Gordon Brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel partnered Oliver Hardy, so his first name stands for one member of that famous duo.

clue.text: Legislator Walker pissed about last two letters from Obama

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the selected pair
someone drunk is all over the place, so the letters of the name are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: spells out that only the final pair of letters of the next word is used

parts.note: the final two letters of Obama

explanation.surface: A politician called Walker gets drunk and rambles on about President Obama.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled WALKER becomes LAW...KER, opened up to take MA from the end of Obama.
explanation.definitionFit: A legislator makes laws, so a lawmaker is the plain English equivalent.

clue.text: Makes you spit, heroin (and hack) — surprised?

parts.note: gob is British slang for spit
smack is slang for heroin
a hack is a journalist, and ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A drug-taking reporter sputters in shock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes you' is just a link joining the pieces; gob is British slang for spit, and a hack is a jobbing journalist, an editor being one kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Gobsmacked is British slang for utterly astonished, so it matches being taken by surprise.

clue.text: (& 9dn.) Straw's success: sod all!

parts.note: His first name with the possessive S
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A sneer at Jack Straw's achievements: they amount to nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Straw is the politician Jack Straw, so his first name plus the S of the possessive starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse slang phrases meaning absolutely nothing; sod all is the British variant.

clue.text: Hotel wife standing by ex-vice-President Ford buggered

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife

indicators.note: something buggered is broken and messed up, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: Al Gore, US vice-president under Clinton
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A wife stands by Gerald Ford, a disgraced former vice-president, in a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Ford really was an ex-vice-president, but here the title is Al Gore and Ford is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Waldorf is a famous luxury hotel, the Waldorf-Astoria in New York or the Waldorf in London.

clue.text: Prescott's no.1 fabric hot bottom support

indicators.note: number one means the first in line, so just the opening letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of Prescott
lint is a soft fabric used for dressings
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Something about John Prescott, the hefty former Deputy PM, and support for his backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth is the base slab on which a statue or column rests, the support at its bottom.

clue.text: " … soft buttocks on heartless beauty …" — don't stop!

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical direction for soft
ass is American slang for the buttocks

indicators.note: without a heart the middle is removed, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: beauty with its middle letters gone

explanation.surface: A breathless quotation from a racy romance, ending with a plea to carry on.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and ellipses make it look like an extract from erotic fiction; the definition is the final instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass by is to go past without halting, which is what someone told not to stop does.

clue.text: Prospect of censure against the President right — not black

indicators.note: the word that follows not is struck out and the word before it takes its place

parts.note: to pan is to criticise harshly
Barack Obama, US President at the time
R is the abbreviation for right
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A prospect of criticism for the President from the political right that is not about race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right – not black' means put right where black was: R and B are the usual abbreviations. Barack Obama was President in 2009.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is a wide unbroken view, and a prospect is likewise an extensive outlook over scenery.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Not the no.1 fictional detective (left out, subject to claims by flipping MPs?)

definitions.text: subject to claims by flipping MPs?

parts.note: whatever is not first is second

indicators.note: out means removed, and left is the abbreviation the solver must drop

parts.note: Sherlock Holmes, Conan Doyle's detective
L is the abbreviation for left; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A detective story twist about not being the top sleuth, with a dig at the MPs' expenses scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 2009 expenses scandal MPs 'flipped' which property they called their second home to maximise claims; HOLMES loses L.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition describes by example: properties MPs designated as secondary residences to claim allowances on, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Wind up bullock's rear — Cyclops departs

indicators.note: the rear is the back end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of bullock
the setter Cyclops refers to himself as I
D is the abbreviation for departs, as in timetables

explanation.surface: A farmyard prank in which someone winds up a bullock and then the setter leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: To kid someone is to tease or fool them, which is what British slang wind up means.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) Gordon, famous familiar political loser, needs ultimate in commiserative drink

parts.note: Gordon Brown, Labour Prime Minister
Al Gore, who famously lost the 2000 US election, known by his familiar first name

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the closing letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of commiserative

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown, a famous loser, needs a commiserating drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown was set to lose the 2010 election; the political loser is the other one, Al Gore.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown ale is a dark, sweetish British beer, so it is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Cameron's right wing spews out (without copier) Mail and Express?

indicators.note: a wing is one end, and with right before it the rightmost letter is meant

parts.note: the rightmost letter of Cameron

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the shuffled letters go round the next item
spewed out suggests letters scattered in disorder

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written, then jumbled
an ape is a copier, one who imitates

explanation.surface: David Cameron's right wing pours out bile in the Tory-supporting Daily Mail and Express.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right wing' reads as Tory politics; it is really the last letter of Cameron. The Daily Mail and Daily Express are British tabloid newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mail and Express are examples of British daily papers, hence the question mark for definition by example.

clue.text: Resemble Nick in need of following

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal or take
after means following

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick needs to imitate a role model.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a name (Nick Clegg, perhaps) but is the British slang verb for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To take after a parent is to look or behave like them, so the phrase is a synonym of resemble.

clue.text: Gloating PM tangled with U Thant about King & I

indicators.note: about means around, so the mixed letters surround the royal pair
things tangled are mixed up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; U Thant was a UN Secretary-General
R for rex, king, plus I

explanation.surface: A smug Prime Minister wrestles with the UN's U Thant over the musical The King and I.
explanation.walkthrough: The King and I is the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical; here King is R (rex) and I is just I.
explanation.definitionFit: Triumphant describes exulting in victory, and gloating is crowing over a win, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Excel in ingenuity: announce Oscar Wilde, say, to be gay

parts.note: to out someone is to announce publicly that they are gay
Oscar Wilde is the classic example of a wit

explanation.surface: A clever person reveals that Oscar Wilde was gay.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'to be gay' complete the sense of the first piece: outing someone means announcing them to be gay.
explanation.definitionFit: To outwit someone is to beat them by being cleverer, which is to excel in ingenuity.

clue.text: VAT — Balls! — possibly increased, getting you pissed

parts.note: a vat is a large tank for liquid
Ed Balls, Labour cabinet minister
up means increased, as in prices up

explanation.surface: Ed Balls might put up VAT, enough to drive anyone to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT looks like the tax but is a large container; Balls is Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanked up is British slang for very drunk, just as pissed is in British usage.

clue.text: Get rich like an expenses-claiming MP profligate (elected)?

definitions.text: Get rich like an expenses-claiming MP

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute, profligate man
an elected candidate is in

explanation.surface: A wasteful MP, once elected, gets rich on expenses.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2009 expenses scandal is the backdrop; the parentheses hold the last piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To rake in money is to accumulate it in large amounts, as MPs fiddling their claims were said to do.

clue.text: Marine's kinky stays

indicators.note: something kinky is twisted, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A soldier's kinky corsetry: stays being the boned undergarment.
explanation.walkthrough: Stays suggests the corset, fitting kinky; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Remains and stays both mean continues to be or is left behind, as verbs in the third person.

clue.text: Magoo-like, rattled PM coy about start of insubordination

indicators.note: about means around, so the shaken letters go round the single letter
something rattled is shaken up, so its letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written, then shaken

indicators.note: start means the very beginning, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of insubordination

explanation.surface: A shaken, evasive Prime Minister fails to see a rebellion coming.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Magoo is the cartoon character famous for being dangerously short-sighted.
explanation.definitionFit: Being short-sighted like the cartoon Mr Magoo is exactly what the medical term myopic means.

clue.text: Some organ on batsman — a real surprise

parts.note: the eye is one organ of the body
an opener is a batsman who opens the innings in cricket

explanation.surface: An organ belonging to a cricket batsman, a shocking discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: Organ invites a sexual or musical reading; it is simply one body part. An opener is one of the first two batsmen in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-opener is a revelation that astonishes, so it amounts to a genuine surprise.

clue.text: Bear Brown's head away — the wreck!

indicators.note: away means gone, so the selected letter is dropped

parts.note: Bruin is a traditional name for a bear

indicators.note: the head is the top, so the first letter of the word is meant

parts.note: the first letter of Brown

explanation.surface: A cry that Gordon Brown has lost his head and wrecked everything.
explanation.walkthrough: Bear Brown suggests a brown bear or bearing Gordon Brown; Bear is Bruin and Brown supplies only the B to lose.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin and wreck are both nouns for something destroyed, or the destruction itself.

clue.text: Squat, shit, dry end

parts.note: a dump is slang for a defecation

indicators.note: the end is the final position, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of dry

explanation.surface: Toilet humour: squatting, defecating and wiping dry at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Squat looks like the posture that goes with the next word; it is the adjective for short and stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumpy means short and thickset, which is what squat means as an adjective.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Character problem, Madonna, at heart

clue.text: On which Gordon's grip is weakening — makes him perspire!

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

clue.text: Many demanding intelligence about Cyclops in the City

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for intelligence wraps the rest

parts.note: nous is common sense or intelligence

explanation.walkthrough: The City suggests London's Square Mile, but here it is ancient Ur; Cyclops is the setter, so he is ME.

the top of a word in a down sense is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Camilla
taken as written, then jumbled
